title: A lock everyone can close
hook: Everyone knows how to lock the message. So why can't everyone unlock it?

doesNotKnow: how a published key can lock but not unlock
that the unlocking key comes from the factors of n

misconception: If everyone knows how to lock a message, everyone can work out how to unlock it.
objective: The learner can explain that with n = 55 and e = 3 anyone can lock m as m^3 mod 55, but unlocking needs d = 27, which comes from 55 = 5 x 11; and that real keys are safe because factoring very large products is not known to be fast.

claims.text: With n = 55 and e = 3, 2 locks to 2^3 mod 55 = 8.
claims.source: 2^3 = 8 < 55. Checked in node by the builder. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): 2^3 = 8 < 55 (node, BigInt).
Arithmetic; d is the inverse of e modulo (p - 1)(q - 1). CLRS 3rd ed. 31.7. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): 4 x 10 = 40; gcd(3, 40) = 1; 3 x 27 = 81 = 2 x 40 + 1. CLRS 3rd ed. 31.7.

claims.text: Unlocking with d = 27 (c^27 mod 55) returns the message, for every message from 0 to 54.
claims.source: Builder's node check: (m^3 mod 55)^27 mod 55 = m for all m in 0..54; e.g. 8^27 mod 55 = 2. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own node BigInt: (m^3)^27 mod 55 = m for all m in 0..54; 8^27 mod 55 = 2.

claims.text: Using e = 3 again does not unlock most messages; for a few toy messages it happens to bring the message back.
claims.source: Builder's node check: m^9 mod 55 = m for 15 of the 55 values (0, 1, 10, 11, 12, 21, 22, 23, 32, 33, 34, 43, 44, 45, 54) and differs for the other 40; e.g. 8^3 mod 55 = 17, not 2. The stage says so when a learner hits one of the 15. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): Own node: m^9 mod 55 = m for exactly the 15 listed values; 8^3 mod 55 = 17. Stage says 'most do not' (40 of 55). Note: 15 of 55 (27%) is more than 'a few'; builder may prefer 'for some toy messages'. Not blocking.

claims.text: Locking needs only n and e; unlocking needs d, and d comes from the factors of n.
claims.source: Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, 'A method for obtaining digital signatures and public-key cryptosystems', CACM 21 (1978); CLRS 3rd ed. 31.7. (d is computed from (p-1)(q-1); knowing d also lets one factor n, so they are equally hard.) | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): RSA (Rivest, Shamir, Adleman, CACM 21(2) 1978): encryption uses (e, n), decryption d, and d = e^-1 mod (p-1)(q-1) needs the factors; computing d is equivalent to factoring. True of the scheme at real sizes. For this toy see c7.

claims.text: No fast method is known for factoring numbers hundreds of digits long, which is the size real keys use.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed. 31.7 and 31.9 (no efficient classical factoring algorithm known; RSA moduli of hundreds of digits). Stated as 'known', not as proven impossible; quantum (Shor) algorithms are out of scope. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 10): No polynomial-time classical factoring algorithm is known (CLRS 3rd ed. 31.7, 31.9); 'known' wording is right; quantum excluded.

claims.text: Predict answer: only someone who knows 55 = 5 x 11 can unlock 8 (locked from 2 with n = 55, e = 3).
claims.source: Unrecorded stage claim (predict question 'Who can unlock 8?', answer 'Only someone who knows 55 = 5 x 11'), recorded by the fact-checker 2026-10-14 (pass 10). CONCERN: false for these numbers. 2^3 = 8 < 55, so the lock never wrapped and anyone takes the ordinary cube root of 8 to get 2 (also true for m = 0..3, own node); and with 55 possible messages anyone with the public key can lock all 55 and look 8 up. The option 'Anyone with the public key' is in fact correct here. Fix (builder): pick a message whose cube exceeds 55 (e.g. m = 7: 343 mod 55 = 13) and reword the question/answer to the realistic case, e.g. 'At real key sizes, who can unlock it?' with 'Only someone who can find d, which needs the factors of n'. Disputed by the fact-checker; needs re-check after the fix.

recall.question: In RSA everyone knows the public numbers n and e. What does someone need to work out the unlocking number d?
options: Just n and e, with enough patience at a calculator
The two primes that multiply to make n
recall.why: d comes from (p - 1)(q - 1), so you need the factors p and q of n. Multiplying them is easy; finding them from n is the hard part.
